pairs.rationale: Jude warns of intruders marked for condemnation who deny the only Master and Lord Jesus Christ. Peter likewise warns of destructive teachers denying the Master who bought them; purchased status, factions and the historical false-prophet comparison are Peter's additional claims.

Paul says God's name is blasphemed among the nations because of his addressees; Peter says the way of truth will be slandered because people follow the teachers' debaucheries. The shared scandal mechanism retains the different objects and groups.

Timothy describes corrupt people treating godliness as a means of gain, while Peter warns of greed exploiting readers through fabricated words. These are specific abuses of religious speech for gain; the passages do not identify the same individuals.

Jude describes angels kept in everlasting chains under gloom for the great day's judgment. Peter describes sinning angels handed over to chains of gloom for judgment after being cast into Tartarus. Their distinct account details and place terminology remain unchanged.

Genesis names Noah, his sons, his wife and his sons' wives entering the ark because of the flood. This supplies the household's narrative setting for Peter's preservation claim; the retained Genesis verse does not enumerate eight or call Noah a herald of righteousness.

Genesis narrates the Lord raining sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah and overturning the cities. Peter recalls their overthrow and adds the explicit function of an example for later ungodly living; that interpretive clause is not inserted into Genesis.

The angels urge Lot's departure and lead him and his household out as the Lord spares him. This is the concrete rescue recalled here; Peter's description of righteous Lot's distress is an additional assessment rather than a quotation of Genesis.

The surrounding men demand Lot's guests, and Lot pleads against acting wickedly. Their narrated conduct supplies context for Peter's account of the lawless deeds Lot encountered; Genesis does not print Peter's day-after-day description of his inner torment.

Paul says God provides a way out with temptation so believers can endure it. Peter says the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial and reserve the unrighteous for judgment. The rescue concern corresponds without equating all trials or omitting Peter's judgment clause.

Jude describes people defiling flesh, rejecting dominion and slandering glorious ones. Peter describes defiling desire, despised lordship and slander of glorious beings, adding recklessness and self-will. The threefold correspondence retains their distinct wording and names no contemporary referents.

Jude gives Michael's refusal to bring a slanderous judgment in his dispute with the devil, leaving rebuke to the Lord. That concrete angelic restraint illustrates the contrast with reckless slander here; Peter does not name Michael or retell that dispute.

Both passages compare the opponents to irrational or unreasoning animals and connect instinctive or uncomprehending behavior with destruction or corruption. Peter adds capture and repeated destruction language; Jude distinguishes what they slander from what they understand by instinct.

Jude calls these participants reefs at the recipients' love feasts and describes fearless feasting and self-shepherding. Peter calls the participants spots and blemishes while feasting with the readers, adding daytime indulgence and harm as wrongdoing's wages. Reefs is preserved rather than changed to blemishes.

The earlier accusation of greed exploiting readers with fabricated words supplies concrete context for the heart trained in greed here. This verse adds adulterous eyes and unstable souls being enticed, so the earlier accusation is not treated as its entire content.

Numbers narrates elders carrying the means of divination and Balaam consulting God about the proposed journey and curse. This gives a concrete solicitation-and-prohibition setting beside Peter's condemnation of Balaam's love of wrongdoing's wages; Numbers does not call these objects fees, and Peter's patronymic remains Bosor.

Numbers says God opened the donkey's mouth, records its speech to Balaam, and gives the angel's rebuke. This is the narrated speaking-beast episode recalled by Peter; the explicit assessment that it restrained the prophet's madness remains Peter's.

Jude compares the opponents to waterless clouds carried by winds and reserves darkness's gloom for wandering stars. Peter uses waterless springs and storm-driven mists and likewise reserves gloom. The differing images are preserved rather than merged into a single quotation.

Jude joins walking according to desires with a mouth speaking boastful things and flattery for advantage. Peter joins inflated words of emptiness to desire-driven enticement, explicitly naming those truly escaping error as endangered. Boastful/inflated wording and truly escaping are preserved.

Jesus calls everyone practicing sin a slave of sin. Peter exposes promised freedom by describing the promisors as corruption's slaves and states that being overcome brings enslavement. The objects sin and corruption correspond without being silently exchanged in the texts.

Jesus' account of the returning unclean spirit ends with a person's last condition becoming worse than the first. Peter gives that same reversal pattern after escape and renewed entanglement; knowledge of Jesus and worldly defilements remain Peter's distinct setting.

Jesus distinguishes the slave who knows his master's will from the one who does not and assigns greater accountability to knowledge. Peter similarly warns of the worse consequence of knowing righteousness and then turning back; their images and specific punishments differ.

The Greek-based proverb says a dog comes upon its vomit and becomes hateful, comparing this with a fool returning in wickedness to his own sin. Peter says the dog returned to its vomit and adds the washed sow returning to mud, absent from this Proverbs unit.

The earlier reminder passage already promises to stir readers who know the truth. Here the writer explicitly describes both letters as stirring a sincere mind by reminders. This connection follows his stated purpose without deriving an external date or identifying a lost letter.

Jude tells readers to remember words spoken beforehand by the apostles of Jesus Christ. Peter likewise asks remembrance of apostolic command and additionally the holy prophets' earlier words; the two instructions overlap without having identical scope.

Jude recalls the warning of mockers in the last time walking according to their ungodly desires. Peter warns of scoffers in the last days following their own desires. The mockers/scoffers wording, time expressions and Jude's additional ungodly description remain distinct.

Ezekiel reports the proverb that the days are far off and vision has perished, then announces God's action without further delay. Peter's scoffers question the coming promise because things appear unchanged. Both challenge confidence in prophetic delay, without identifying the two audiences or events.

Genesis narrates God speaking the firmament, separating waters and gathering them so dry land appears, naming Heaven and Earth. These water-and-word creation acts illuminate Peter's account of heavens and earth formed through water by God's word, while the precise descriptions remain distinct.

Genesis narrates the flood's destruction of living creatures and preservation of Noah and those with him. Peter recalls the former world's watery destruction, without making this narrative claim that every created thing or Noah himself perished.

The following account specifies the fiery dissolution of heavens and elements at the coming day. It expands the stored-for-fire expectation here; the earth's works not being found in verse10 is preserved rather than replaced by a burned-up reading.

The Psalm compares a thousand years in God's sight to yesterday passing and a night watch. Peter repeats the thousand-years/day comparison and explicitly states it in both directions. Neither passage supplies a formula for calculating a date of the coming.

Paul says God's kindness leads toward repentance in a context of kindness, restraint and patience. Peter interprets apparent delay as patience aimed at repentance rather than destruction. The comparison concerns the purpose of patience, without erasing their differing recipients and arguments.

Paul likewise says the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. Peter uses the thief comparison and adds cosmic dissolution and works not being found; those additions are not ascribed to this Thessalonians verse.

The earlier letter requires holiness in all conduct and invokes impartial judgment during the readers' sojourn. Peter here asks what holy conduct and godliness should accompany anticipated dissolution. Their practical call to holiness corresponds, while the immediate grounds differ.

The earlier description of the day of the Lord already names heavens passing and elements dissolved by heat. This verse repeats the fiery cosmic horizon while adding waiting for and hastening the day of God; no calculation or mechanism for hastening is supplied.

Isaiah announces that heaven will be new and earth new; Peter awaits new heavens and a new earth according to a promise and adds that righteousness dwells there. Heaven/heavens and Isaiah's statement about former things remain distinct.

Paul prays for the recipients to be kept blameless at Jesus' coming; Peter urges diligence to be found spotless and blameless in peace while awaiting these things. Prayer and exhortation preserve distinct agency and wording within a shared expectation.

Paul's explicit account of divine patience directed toward repentance provides a concrete comparison with considering the Lord's patience salvation. Peter names Paul here, but this thematic connection does not prove which particular letter he means or that this is a quotation.

The earlier warning describes destructive teaching and swift destruction; here distortion of difficult Pauline passages and other Scriptures leads to the distorters' own destruction. The shared danger is specific, while neither verse establishes that every difficult reading is intentional falsification.

Ephesians warns against being carried about by every wind of teaching through human trickery and cunning in deceitful schemes. Peter warns against being carried away by lawless error and falling from firmness. The specific instability comparison does not identify all their opponents as one group.

The opening blessing joins multiplied grace and peace with knowledge of God and Jesus; the close commands growth in grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ. This forms a concrete opening-and-closing correspondence, with the concluding glory ascription remaining additional.
